messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Chaplain
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Crowding: Crowded places, Auditory (Breathing): Heavy breathing sounds
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Vinh's Recurrence

Vinh was thirty-four when the two men cornered him in the parking garage behind the hospital where he worked as a chaplain. It was a Tuesday evening in March, nearly two years ago, and he had stayed late to sit with a dying patient's family. The garage was half-empty, fluorescent lights casting long shadows between the concrete pillars. He was walking toward his car when he heard the footsteps quicken behind him—two sets, closing in fast. One of them had a knife. They wanted his wallet, his phone, his watch. When he hesitated, one of them grabbed his collar and slammed him against the pillar. The other pressed the blade against his ribs and told him to stop being stupid. Vinh remembered the smell of stale cigarettes and something chemical—maybe cologne, maybe sweat—and the sound of his own breathing, ragged and panicked, competing with their harsh commands. They took everything. He was not seriously injured, but the violation left him hollowed out in a way the bruises never quite explained.

In the weeks after, Vinh had tried to return to his chaplaincy work. But something had shifted. When he walked through the hospital corridors now, particularly the parking garage, his body would tense. He began noticing people—really noticing them, assessing them. Anyone who vaguely resembled one of his attackers would trigger a cascade of images: the knife, the hand at his collar, the blur of the pillar rushing toward his face. These were not fleeting thoughts; they were vivid, intrusive pictures that flooded his awareness with photographic clarity. The visual memories came unbidden, especially when he encountered men in crowds or in confined spaces like the garage. Over time, Vinh had come to believe that the event had revealed something true about himself—that he was the kind of person who invited predation, who lacked the instinct to protect himself or to read danger correctly. If he had been more alert, more assertive, more like other men, he would have seen them coming. Somebody else would have fought back or run. This conviction, once formed, began to color how he interpreted every reminder of the attack. When he caught sight of someone who resembled one of the men, or when he found himself in a crowded place, that negative appraisal would activate first: *I am the sort of person this happens to.* And immediately, the sensory memories would flood in—the smell, the images, the feeling of helplessness.

The heaviness of these appraisals deepened his isolation. Vinh became convinced that he could not stop bad things from happening to him, that some essential fragility had been exposed. This belief made him hypervigilant in ways that exhausted him. He began avoiding the hospital parking garage entirely, taking the long route through the main entrance even in bad weather. He avoided crowded spaces—the hospital cafeteria, the chapel during services, even the grocery store on weekends. But avoidance only seemed to sharpen his sensitivity. When he did encounter a crowded place—unavoidably, at a colleague's funeral reception—the press of bodies around him triggered both the intrusive images and a surge of rage so intense it frightened him. He could feel the old smell in his nostrils, see the faces looming, and underneath it all was a burning fury at himself for being the kind of man this could happen to, for being powerless. The rage and the images fed each other; remembering the event flooded him with anger at his own perceived weakness, and that anger seemed to sharpen the sensory details even further.

His wife, Maya, had died of cancer just eight months before the mugging. Vinh had been grieving, but functional—his chaplaincy work had given him purpose in that darkness. After the attack, he found himself unable to access even that solace. He stopped attending the hospital's informal support groups. He began calling in sick. The one person who might have helped him carry this—Maya—was already gone. He sat alone in their apartment most evenings now, and when he closed his eyes, he could smell the garage, see the knife, feel the rage at himself for being so utterly, irredeemably powerless. It was this combination—the vivid, intrusive memories; the conviction that he was fundamentally flawed; the certainty that he could not protect himself from harm—that finally brought him to seek help. He was afraid that without intervention, he would disappear entirely into the narrow, controlled world he had built to avoid triggering the cycle again. What he hoped for, though he barely dared articulate it, was to feel like a chaplain again rather than a victim, and to believe that not all bad things were inevitable consequences of who he was.
